symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with characteristic concentric rings (target spot appearance) on older leaves.
Yellow halo surrounding leaf lesions leading to premature defoliation.
Sunken, leathery dark spots near the stem end of fruits.
causes: Warm temperatures (24°C to 29°C) combined with high humidity or prolonged leaf wetness.
Fungal spores overwintering in infected plant debris and soil.
Splashing water from rainfall or overhead irrigation spreading spores to lower leaves.
prevention: Rotate crops with non-solanaceous crops (e.g., corn, beans) for 2–3 years.
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering to keep foliage dry.
Mulch soil around plants to prevent soil-borne spores from splashing onto foliage.

organic: Apply Copper Octanoate or Copper Hydroxide spray every 7–10 days.
Prune lower leaves (bottom 12 inches) to improve air circulation.

symptoms: Olive-green to dull brown velvety spots on young leaves and fruit.
Deformed, cracked fruit with corky brown scabby patches.
Yellowing leaves dropping prematurely in mid-summer.
causes: Cool, wet spring weather allowing ascopores to germinate on fresh leaf tissue.
Fungus overwintering in fallen dead leaves under orchard trees.
prevention: Rake and destroy or compost fallen apple leaves in autumn.
Prune trees annually to open the canopy for sun and air drying.
Plant resistant apple varieties (e.g., Liberty, Enterprise, Freedom).

organic: Apply Liquid Lime Sulfur or Potassium Bicarbonate before leaf wetness events.
Neem oil spray during green tip and cluster stages.

symptoms: Vibrant green leaf blade free of chlorosis, necrosis, or leaf spots.
Strong structural integrity with clear parallel venation.
prevention: Maintain regular soil testing and crop monitoring.

organic: No treatment required. Continue good agronomic practices.

symptoms: Small, water-soaked dark green spots on leaves turning brown with yellow borders.
Leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely, exposing fruit to sunscald.
Raised, scab-like rough spots on green fruit.
causes: Warm, rainy, and windy conditions spreading bacteria through water droplets.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants.
Avoid overhead irrigation and working in wet fields.

organic: Fixed copper sprays combined with bio-bactericides.
Remove and burn infected foliage promptly.
chemical: Copper Hydroxide mixed with Mancozeb (improves bactericidal efficacy).
Streptomycin sulfate (where registered for agricultural use).

symptoms: Large, dark brown to purplish-black water-soaked lesions on leaf tips and margins.
White moldy fungal growth visible on the underside of leaves during humid weather.
Rapid rot and collapse of entire canopy; foul decay odor.
causes: Cool, moist weather (15°C to 20°C with >90% humidity).
Infected seed tubers or volunteer potato plants.
prevention: Hill up soil around plants to protect tubers from spores.
Destroy volunteer potato plants and nightshade weeds.

organic: Preventative copper hydroxide sprays before weather turns cool and wet.
Destroy and remove severely infected vines.
